```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5,
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(tidyr)
data.table::setDTthreads(1L)
options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE, scipen = 999, digits = 4)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
```

`aggregate_estimands()` averages the treatment-group-specific estimates of `multiple_treatment_group_analysis()` across treatment groups, by event time (Section 5 of Leventer 2025, [*Identification of Child Penalties*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07486)). Symbols and row labels are in [Notation and output](notation.html), the estimators and influence functions in [Estimation](estimators.html). Equation, section and theorem numbers refer to the main text; appendices are referred to by name.

The examples use one simulated panel. Treatment groups 24-30 at event times 0-3 use control groups up to 34, so every treatment group has a cell at every event time.

```{r estimate}
library(childpen)
sim <- simulate_data(20000, 24:34)
res <- multiple_treatment_group_analysis(sim, 24:30, periods_post = 3,
                                         periods_pre = NULL, verbose = FALSE)
```

The result carries the person-level influence functions that `aggregate_estimands()` reads, so it is passed on unmodified.

## 1. Aggregate causal estimands

For event time $e$, let $\mathcal{D}(e) = \{d : d + e < D_{\max}\}$ be the treatment groups that have an estimate. Since the control group is $d' = d + e + 1$, the condition is $d' \le D_{\max}$, the bound set by `max_control_group`. With $\mathbb{E}_D$ the expectation over the treatment distribution, Section 5.1 defines

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{Agg}}(e) = \mathbb{E}_D\big[\rho(D, D, D + e) - \rho(D, \infty, D + e) \mid D + e < D_{\max}\big] \qquad \text{(eq. (10))},
$$
$$
\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},1}(g, e) = \mathbb{E}_D\big[\theta(g, D, D + e) \mid G = g,\, D + e < D_{\max}\big],
$$
$$
\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},2}(g, e) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_D\big[\mathrm{ATE}(g, D, D + e) \mid G = g,\, D + e < D_{\max}\big]}{\mathbb{E}_D\big[\mathrm{APO}(g, D, \infty, D + e) \mid G = g,\, D + e < D_{\max}\big]},
$$
$$
\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{Agg}}(e) = \mathbb{E}_D\big[\theta(f, D, D + e) - \theta(m, D, D + e) \mid D + e < D_{\max}\big] \qquad \text{(eq. (11))}.
$$

The package replaces each treatment-group causal estimand by its 2x2 descriptive counterpart $B_d$ and the treatment distribution by weights $w_d$ (next section), so that $\hat A(e) = \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}(e)} w_d \hat B_d$. The rows of `aggregate_estimands()` are identified by `method`, `estimand` and `agg_type`:

| `method` | `estimand` | `agg_type` | aggregate | $B_d$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DID_Female`, `DID_Male` | `theta` | `weighted_avg` | $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},1}(g, e)$ | $\delta_\theta(g)$ |
| `DID_Female`, `DID_Male` | `theta` | `ratio_of_avgs` | $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},2}(g, e)$ | $\delta_{\mathrm{ATE}}(g)$ and $\delta_{\mathrm{APO}}(g)$, averaged separately and divided |
| `NTD` | `rho_effect` | `weighted_avg` | $\rho_{\mathrm{Agg}}(e)$ | $\delta_{\Delta\rho}$ |
| `Conventional` | `gap_theta` | `weighted_avg` | $\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{Agg}}(e)$ | $\delta_{\Delta\theta}$ |
| `TD_E_LOGS` | `rho_effect` | `weighted_avg` | $\rho_{\mathrm{Agg}}(e)$ under TD-E-LOGS | $\delta_{\Delta\rho}$ with $\delta^{\times}_{\mathrm{APO}}$ |
| `TD`, `TD_PR`, accounting rows of `NTD` and `TD_E_LOGS` | `gap_ATE`, `gap_theta_pre`, `rho_obs`, `rho_cf`, `share_parenthood`, `share_other` | `weighted_avg` | weighted average of the group-level row; no symbol in the paper | the group-level row |

The output has one row per event time, `control_offset`, `estimand`, `method` and `agg_type`, with `est`, `se`, `n_groups` (treatment groups with positive weight), `ci_l`, `ci_h`, `t` and `p`.

```{r agg-rows}
agg <- aggregate_estimands(res)
agg |>
  filter(event_time == 2, estimand %in% c("theta", "gap_theta", "rho_effect"),
         method %in% c("DID_Female", "Conventional", "NTD")) |>
  select(method, estimand, agg_type, est, se, n_groups)
```

**$\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},1}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},2}$.** Writing $\mathrm{ATE}(g) = \theta(g)\,\mathrm{APO}(g, \infty)$, Section 5.1 shows that $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},2}$ is also a weighted average of the $\theta(g, d, d + e)$, with weights
$$
w(g, d, e) = \frac{p(g, d, e)\,\mathrm{APO}(g, d, \infty, d + e)}{\sum_{k:\, k + e < D_{\max}} p(g, k, e)\,\mathrm{APO}(g, k, \infty, k + e)}, \qquad p(g, d, e) = \Pr(D = d \mid G = g,\, D + e < D_{\max}).
$$
Where $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},1}$ weights by the treatment distribution, $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},2}$ weights by the treatment distribution times the counterfactual APO, so treatment groups with higher counterfactual earnings receive more weight; the paper notes these are typically the later-treated groups. The paper takes $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},1}$ as the preferable aggregate estimand for this reason (Section 5.1).

```{r theta-agg}
agg |>
  filter(method == "DID_Female", estimand == "theta") |>
  select(event_time, agg_type, est) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = agg_type, values_from = est)
```

**Aggregating before or after differencing.** For the gender gap, Section 5.1 aggregates the within-group difference, $\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{Agg}}(e)$, rather than differencing the two within-gender aggregates, $\theta_{\mathrm{Agg},1}(f, e) - \theta_{\mathrm{Agg},1}(m, e)$. The two coincide only when the male and female treatment distributions are identical, and the second confounds differences in group-specific effects with gender differences in the treatment distribution. Accordingly `Conventional` (like `NTD`) uses weights pooled over genders, while `DID_Female` and `DID_Male` use weights within gender.

## 2. Weights

| `weights` | weight of treatment group $d$ in $\mathcal{D}(e)$ |
|---|---|
| `"sample"` (default) | the share of persons in the group: $w_d = n_d / \sum_{k \in \mathcal{D}(e)} n_k$, where $n_d$ counts persons of both genders with $D = d$. For `DID_Female` and `DID_Male`, shares within gender: $w_{g,d} = n_{g,d} / \sum_{k \in \mathcal{D}(e)} n_{g,k}$ |
| `"uniform"` or `NULL` | $1/m_e$, with $m_e$ the number of groups in $\mathcal{D}(e)$ |
| a named numeric vector | proportional to the entry named $d$, renormalized to sum to one over $\mathcal{D}(e)$. Groups missing from the vector get weight zero, with a warning |

```{r weights}
w_named <- setNames(dnorm(24:30, mean = 27, sd = 3), 24:30)
bind_rows(
  sample  = aggregate_estimands(res, weights = "sample",  methods = "NTD"),
  uniform = aggregate_estimands(res, weights = "uniform", methods = "NTD"),
  named   = aggregate_estimands(res, weights = w_named,   methods = "NTD"),
  .id = "weights"
) |>
  filter(estimand == "rho_effect", event_time %in% c(0, 3)) |>
  select(weights, event_time, est, se, n_groups)
```

**Groups that drop out.** A treatment group has a cell at event time $e$ only if its control group $d + e + 1$ is at most `max_control_group` ($D_{\max}$ in the paper). Groups beyond the bound drop out at later event times, and `n_groups` records how many remain.

```{r dmax}
res_cap <- multiple_treatment_group_analysis(sim, 24:30, periods_post = 3, periods_pre = NULL,
                                             max_control_group = 32, verbose = FALSE)
bind_rows(
  `Inf` = aggregate_estimands(res,     methods = "NTD"),
  `32`  = aggregate_estimands(res_cap, methods = "NTD"),
  .id = "max_control_group"
) |>
  filter(estimand == "rho_effect") |>
  select(max_control_group, event_time, est, n_groups)
```

With `max_control_group = 32`, group 30 has cells at $e = 0, 1$ only and group 29 at $e \le 2$, so $\mathcal{D}(e)$ shrinks and the weights change with $e$. As the footnote to eq. (10) notes (following Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021), a comparison of aggregates across $e$ then combines variation in causal effects with a shift in the composition of treatment groups. The composition is the same at every event time when each group in the aggregate has a cell at each of them, as with `max_control_group = Inf` above (`n_groups` is 7 throughout).

## 3. Standard errors

Let $B_d$ be the estimate of treatment group $d$, $p_d = \Pr(D = d)$ its population share, $P_e = \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}(e)} p_d$ and $w_d = p_d / P_e$. The influence function of $A(e) = \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}(e)} w_d B_d$ is (the aggregate estimator section of the appendix on estimation and inference)
$$
\psi_{A(e)} = \frac{1}{P_e} \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}(e)} \Big[ \big(B_d - A(e)\big)\,\psi_{p_d} + p_d\,\psi_{B_d} \Big], \qquad \psi_{p_d} = 1\{D = d\} - p_d .
$$
For the within-gender rows the share is the joint share of gender $g$ and group $d$, with $1\{G = g, D = d\} - p_{g,d}$ in place of $\psi_{p_d}$. With `"uniform"` or fixed weights the first term is absent; with `"sample"` it accounts for the estimated shares. For `ratio_of_avgs` the chain rule is applied to the ratio of the two weighted averages, each with its share term, and the influence function of `share_other` is minus that of `share_parenthood`.

The group-level influence functions are summed per person across treatment groups before they are squared, with clusters at the person level,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat A) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{c} \Big( \sum_{i \in c} \hat\psi_i \Big)^2 \frac{G}{G - 1},
$$
for $n$ person-age rows and $G$ persons. A person who serves as a control group member for several treatment groups therefore enters several terms of the same sum. The share term is put on the person-age scale with the average number of ages per person, which is exact for a balanced panel. The estimators and the influence functions of the group-level rows are in [Estimation](estimators.html).

The table compares the `se` of `aggregate_estimands()` under uniform weights with $\sqrt{\sum_d w_d^2\,\mathrm{se}_d^2}$, the standard error if the group-level estimates were independent. The latter is also the calculation used, with a warning, when `results` has lost its influence-function attributes (for example a table read back from a file).

```{r se}
agg_u <- aggregate_estimands(res, weights = "uniform", methods = "NTD") |>
  filter(estimand == "rho_effect") |>
  select(event_time, est, se)
indep <- res |>
  filter(method == "NTD", estimand == "rho_effect") |>
  group_by(event_time) |>
  summarise(se_independent = sqrt(sum(se^2)) / n())
left_join(agg_u, indep, by = "event_time")
```

## 4. Pre-treatment event times

With `include_pre = TRUE`, pre-treatment event times are aggregated as well. A pre-treatment event time has one cell per control group, $d' = d + 1, \dots, d + H + 1$, and each `control_offset` $d' - d$ is aggregated separately, so each row is the aggregate of the validation estimates of one treatment-control distance. (After treatment `control_offset` equals `event_time` + 1, and each event time has one aggregate.) With the default `pre = 1` and `periods_pre = K`, the pre-treatment event times are $-(1 + K), \dots, -2$; the baseline is $e = -1$.

```{r pre}
res_pre <- multiple_treatment_group_analysis(sim, 26:28, periods_post = 2, periods_pre = 2,
                                             verbose = FALSE)
agg_pre <- aggregate_estimands(res_pre, include_pre = TRUE,
                               methods = c("DID_Female", "Conventional"))
agg_pre |>
  filter(event_time < 0, agg_type == "weighted_avg") |>
  mutate(row = paste(method, estimand, sep = " / "),
         control_offset = factor(control_offset)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = event_time, y = est, ymin = ci_l, ymax = ci_h, color = control_offset)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
  facet_wrap(~ row) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:-2) +
  labs(x = "Event time", y = "Aggregate estimate", color = "Control offset") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Under no anticipation, a zero pre-treatment `DID_Female` or `DID_Male` `theta` corresponds to $\gamma_{\mathrm{PT}}(g) = 0$ and a zero `Conventional` `gap_theta` to the NTD-PT restriction at that age (Lemma 1 and Proposition 1 of the paper).

## 5. Comparing aggregates across strata

Studies compute aggregates within a stratum, such as a country or a parent type, and compare them across strata (Section 5.2). An aggregate depends on the treatment distribution: strata with different distributions of age at first birth give different aggregates even when the treatment-group-specific effects are the same, for example when parents have children earlier in one country than in another and early treatment groups receive more weight.

Figure 9 of the paper illustrates this. It keeps the treatment-group-specific estimates of the effect of parenthood on the gender earnings ratio fixed, and aggregates them with three treatment distributions, normal densities with standard deviation 3 and means 26, 29 and 32 over the treatment groups $D \in [24, 34]$ (right-skewed, centered, left-skewed). The same exercise with the simulated group estimates `res`, with means 24, 27 and 30 over the treatment groups 24-30 (three years either side of the middle of the range, as in the paper):

```{r strata-weights}
groups <- 24:30
means  <- c("Right-skewed" = 24, "Centered" = 27, "Left-skewed" = 30)
W <- sapply(means, function(m) dnorm(groups, mean = m, sd = 3))
rownames(W) <- groups
round(prop.table(W, margin = 2), 3)   # weights after normalization
```

```{r strata}
by_dist <- lapply(names(means), function(nm) {
  w <- setNames(W[, nm], groups)
  aggregate_estimands(res, weights = w, methods = "NTD") |>
    filter(estimand == "rho_effect") |>
    mutate(distribution = factor(nm, levels = names(means)))
}) |>
  bind_rows()

ggplot(by_dist, aes(x = event_time, y = est, ymin = ci_l, ymax = ci_h)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ distribution) +
  labs(x = "Event time", y = expression(rho[Agg](e)))
```

The three panels average the same treatment-group estimates; only the weights differ. Figure 9 and the cross-country figure of the appendix on aggregate estimates (Israel, the UK and Germany) are in [Replicating the paper](replication.html).
